The question is therefore asked of the RESPONSE and the chip's subject is no longer an operand of `reconciledPartnerName` at all — the fix is structural rather than a second rule to keep in step. The set is `chipSubjectRows`: the substances the QUESTION put in play, plus the active-order substances where the screening arm will run, each represented by the row `SubstanceSubjects.subjectOf` elects, resolved once in `validate` before any arm words a chip and memoised per co-medication for the pass (`CoMedications.displayNamesAnotherChipSubject`). The comparison is through `DrugReference.matchesDrugName` — CLAUDE.md's accessor for a clinician-entered drug NAME against an entry, which is what an order display is.

Three parts, each with its own case and each mutated at review round 4's head — before the round-7 revert below removed the mechanism, so none of these three mutations can be reproduced at this head at all — with the counts taken from that round's test set: refusing nothing reddened three cases — `aPrescriptionThatNamesTheSubjectDoesNotNameThePartner`, `twoSubjectsNameOneCombinationPrescriptionTheSameWay` and `aScreeningQuestionRefusesACombinationDisplayThatNamesAnotherOrdersDrug`; dropping the partner's-own-substance exclusion reddened `theScreeningArmStillNamesAnOrderByItsOwnDisplay`, the two combination cases refusing either way (without it the screening arm would refuse every order whose display names the drug it IS, which is every order — the whole of what this decision gave that arm); dropping the screening rows reddened `aScreeningQuestionRefusesACombinationDisplayThatNamesAnotherOrdersDrug`. Stated as what each mutation reached, not as what it left alone: none of the three can be re-measured at this head, so an exclusivity claim about them is one no reader can check. The shipped-KB arrangement above is pinned as agreement rather than against a literal by `aCombinationOrderOnTheShippedKnowledgeBaseIsNamedOneWay`.

**The QUESTION's drugs and not the drugs in play**, for `namingRows`' own reason: the pre-answer findings pass validates with an EMPTY answer and the chips pass with the real one, so a set built from `inPlay` could refuse in one pass and permit in the other, and the citable `safety_finding` the model read would name a prescription differently from the chip beside the answer. **Nothing in the suite pins that choice** — measured, reading `inPlay` there leaves the whole api build green — and the residue it leaves is that a subject only the ANSWER named can still be named by the prescription its own chip's partner came from, so that chip still reads as a self-interaction. Consistent across the response and across the two passes, which is what the set is for.

Scoped to this rung deliberately: the ENTRY rung prints a dataset name for one substance the token must claim unambiguously first, and the `!namesADrug` rung prints the rule's own token, so neither can put a prescription display in front of a clinician.

**Superseded by review round 7, which removed the refusal.** **And the refusal is a RECONCILIATION onto the rule's token, not a null** (review round 5). Rounds 3 and 4 answered null, and null means "each sentence keeps the name its own arm resolved" — so the FOLD, which calls `reconciledPartnerName` directly, put the rule sentence on `partnerLabel` while its class sentence kept `classPartnerName`'s label. One detail then named one prescription two ways, which is #292's own invariant and the one the ticket says is currently held (*"one chip never contradicts itself"*). It was a REGRESSION against the merge base rather than a residue inherited from it, because the merge base's fold had no such refusal reason: measured through the real `validate` over the shipped KB, one ordinary `Amlodipine / Atorvastatin` order (codes `C10BX03`, uncovered, and `C10AA05`) asked *"Can I give her amlodipine and simvastatin?"* read `Simvastatin interacts with active order atorvastatin — Moderate. … Simvastatin is in the same ATC class (C10AA) as active order Amlodipine / Atorvastatin`, where `abb36813` printed the display in both. So the rung returns `ReconciledPartner(token, token)` — outcome 1's shape, reached for a different reason — and both sentences take the one name every unfolded chip about that co-medication already prints. `aFoldedChipRefusingACombinationDisplayNamesThePrescriptionOnce` (fixture) and `aFoldedChipOnTheShippedKnowledgeBaseNamesTheCombinationOnce` (shipped KB) are the cases that redden when that branch answers null again — with `aClassOnlyChipRefusesTheDisplayTheRuleChipsRefused` since review round 6 carried the same refusal to the class arm's own sentence, so a null here splits its folded chip the other way about; those three and no others, re-measured at this head. Refusing nothing still reddens round 4's three.

The token and never the dataset's name for `OrderPartner.labelEntry`, which two things decide: this rung has proved nothing about that entry (`nameByOrder` does not update it, so the ENTRY rung's `unambiguouslyNames` is deliberately not asked here), and the token is what round 4's cases pin every unfolded chip about such a partner on — a dataset name here would name the prescription one way on a folded chip and another on an unfolded one, which is the defect one level along. Never a bare ATC code either: `namesNamingOrder` is false for a token-less rule, so `partnerLabel` can only be the token on this path (#155/#290, Decisions 38 and 39). What it costs is outcome 1's cost on strictly stronger evidence — the class sentence's subject moves from the prescription to what the token names, so where the shared subgroup was matched through a code the dataset cannot name the stated class need not classify the drug the sentence names (#161's shape, already accepted at outcome 1 — **but NOT by `OrderPartner.nameByOrder`, which is review round 7's correction (2) below: that method prefers the order's display precisely so that a partly-covered partner is not named by a constituent, so naming one is the defect it exists to prevent and not a trade it licenses**); stronger because `namesNamingOrder` has already proved the token names that very prescription, which outcome 1 cannot say. **A class-ONLY chip about that prescription took the ladder's label until review round 6**, having no token for any gate to read — and that was NOT the ROW residue the bullet below states, which is the ENTRY rung's and is conditioned per RULE. This one's condition is the PRESCRIPTION's and the RESPONSE's, which is what round 4 restructured it to be, so a class-only chip can read it; see the round-6 paragraph below.

**Superseded by review round 7, which removed the refusal from both sites.** **And the class arm's own sentence asks the same refusal** (review round 6). Rounds 3, 4 and 5 applied it only where a rule was in hand, so `classPartnerName` — the class-ONLY chip's whole detail, and a folded chip's class sentence where `reconciledPartnerName` declines — went on printing `OrderPartner.label`, the prescription's display. One response therefore printed the prescription as the rule's token on its rule chips and as its full display on its class-only ones: measured at this head through the real `validate` over `DrugReferenceTestSupport.shippedEntries()`, one `Dolutegravir / Lamivudine` order (codes `J05AR25`, uncovered, and `J05AF05`) asked *"Can I give her dolutegravir, emtricitabine and entecavir?"* printed `Emtricitabine interacts with active order lamivudine — Major. … Emtricitabine is in the same ATC class (J05AF) as active order lamivudine` beside `Entecavir is in the same ATC class (J05AF) as active order Dolutegravir / Lamivudine`, where the merge base `abb36813` printed the display in all three (measured there, in a worktree) — a REGRESSION against the base, and it re-creates the ticket's shape (b) as well: the same Emtricitabine × Lamivudine pair reads `Dolutegravir / Lamivudine` for *"Can I give her emtricitabine and entecavir?"* and `lamivudine` once the question also names dolutegravir. **This is not the ROW residue the trade-off bullet below records** and the round-5 paragraph above mis-filed it as that: that one is the ENTRY rung, a divergence between two ROWS of one substance on a condition that is per RULE (the token claiming one row and not the other), which no class-only chip can read. This refusal's condition is a property of the whole partner and of the response — round 4's own restructuring — so every chip can read it, and `classPartnerName` now does.

What it takes instead is the rung the ladder used BEFORE `OrderPartner.nameByOrder`: the dataset's name for the substance `soleSubstanceOf` resolved, elected by this response (`SubstanceSubjects.subjectOf`) — which is exactly what that method already prints for a partner no order renamed, so a refusal returns the ORDER rung to the ENTRY rung rather than inventing a fourth name. Never the rule's token: a class-only chip has none, and borrowing another chip's would state the class relationship this arm found for one substance about a drug it did not resolve, which is `reconciledPartnerName`'s last branch. So the two surfaces name one SUBSTANCE in the knowledge base's two vocabularies, the match token and the row's display — the residue an ENTRY-rung refusal already leaves, and a pure case difference in the Dovato arrangement (`lamivudine` against `Lamivudine`). The class-only chip's own text therefore MOVES, and it is prompt-visible in the same way every other chip here is — `DrugReferenceInjector.renderFinding` copies the detail verbatim into a citable `safety_finding`. Decision 39's name-union bound is already retired by this decision (see the trade-off bullet), so nothing here rests on it; what the movement replaces is a prescription display the same prompt still carries on its own `active_drug_order` record. Measured over the shipped knowledge base through the real `validate`, 500 synthetic fixed-dose arrangements each raising a rule chip and a class-only chip about one combination order whose display names another subject of the same response (order display `<rule subject> / <the code's first entry>`, codes `{J05AR25, that code}`, question naming the rule subject and a rule-less class sibling): the refused display is printed in **500 before this round and 0 after**, and the class sentence disagrees case-insensitively with every rule chip's name for the same prescription in **500 before and 70 after**. Of those 70, **63 have one of the two names inside the other** (`Meticillin (methicillin)` against the token `methicillin`, `Dipivefrin (ophthalmic)` against `dipivefrin`) and **7 are unrelated strings**, every one of them the harness's own shape where the rule the chip carries is about the OTHER half of the combination (`Abacavir / Ezetimibe`, token `abacavir`, ladder entry `Ezetimibe`) — there each sentence names the constituent its own claim is about where before one of them named the whole product, which is #161's accepted trade (`OrderPartner.nameByOrder`) rather than a new one. `aClassOnlyChipRefusesTheDisplayTheRuleChipsRefused` (fixture, which pins the vocabulary residue as a literal), `aClassOnlyChipOnTheShippedKnowledgeBaseRefusesTheRefusedDisplay` and `aFoldDeclinedForOneReasonStillHonoursTheResponsesRefusal` are the pins, and the only three cases in the api suite that redden when the conjunct is dropped (measured at review round 6's head; round 7 removed both the conjunct and all three of those cases, so nothing here is reproducible at this head). **The third is where the two refusal reasons COMPOSE**, and it is the one arrangement in which round 6 is not a case difference: the ORDER rung declines because the rule's token does not name the prescription (the `naproxen`-rule-under-an-`Esomeprazole 20mg`-order shape), the fold therefore words its class sentence from `classPartnerName`, and before this round that sentence printed `Esomeprazole 20mg` — a class relationship found through naproxen's own ATC code, under a proton-pump inhibitor's prescription, which is the very mis-attribution the rule sentence beside it had just refused. It now reads `naproxen` / `Naproxen`. The merge base printed `Esomeprazole 20mg` there as well (measured through the same fixture in a worktree at `abb36813`), so that arrangement is an improvement on both heads rather than a regression repaired — unlike the two class-only cases, where the base named the prescription once.

**Three corrections to the paragraph above, from review round 7, before the whole mechanism was reverted.** They are recorded because two of them are reasoning errors a reader could repeat, not merely statements the revert made moot. (2) The 7 unrelated-string residue was filed as *"#161's accepted trade (`OrderPartner.nameByOrder`)"* and that INVERTS its own precedent: `nameByOrder` prefers the order's display precisely so a partly-covered partner is NOT named by a constituent, because that produces "a chip whose stated class does not classify the drug it names"; what #161/Decision 38 accept is the NAMELESS-order case and (#293) the free-text-disagreement case. `reconciledPartnerName`'s ORDER-rung comment made the same mis-citation. (3) The cases named as the pins for rounds 3 to 6 — `aPrescriptionThatNamesTheSubjectDoesNotNameThePartner`, `aScreeningQuestionRefusesACombinationDisplayThatNamesAnotherOrdersDrug`, `aFoldedChipRefusingACombinationDisplayNamesThePrescriptionOnce`, `aClassOnlyChipRefusesTheDisplayTheRuleChipsRefused`, `aClassOnlyChipOnTheShippedKnowledgeBaseRefusesTheRefusedDisplay`, `aFoldDeclinedForOneReasonStillHonoursTheResponsesRefusal` and `anOrderTheDatasetCoversNoEntryForKeepsItsOwnDisplayEvenWhenRefused` — no longer exist under those names; five were rewritten to assert the invariant rather than the mechanism (see the round-7 paragraphs for what each became) and two were removed, one because its whole subject was the screened-order leg of `chipSubjectRows` and one because its residue is already pinned as WRONG by `NonCodedDrugOrderNameTest.aClassChipCanNameAnOrderAfterTextTheCitedSubgroupDoesNotClassify`. Two new cases were added (`PartialOrderCoveragePartnerTest` ×2, above) as two were removed, so the api suite's total is the same either side of round 7 and a count is no evidence here — no absolute is quoted for it, because merging `main` moves the total without touching this change (it read 1664 at round 7's head and 1683 once PR #345 merged in at round 8's).

**Review round 7: the refusal is removed, because every name it could step back to is a CONSTITUENT name and a constituent cannot carry the class sentence.** The ORDER rung is reached only for a partner holding a code the loaded dataset can name no entry for (`OrderPartner.nameByOrder`), and `classRelationships` cites its shared subgroup over ALL of the partner's codes — so where the subgroup came from that uncovered code, neither `soleSubstanceOf`'s substance (what round 6 printed) nor the rule's own token (what round 5 printed) publishes it, and the chip states a class membership false of the drug it names. That is the chip `nameByOrder`'s own javadoc exists to prevent — "naming the merged partner Rifapentine produces …is in the same ATC class (J04AC) as active order Rifapentine" — i.e. #161's right-finding-wrong-reason shape, which the Decision-39 paragraph above already calls a false claim and accepts only for a builder-unreachable blank display. Rounds 5 and 6 handed it to every partly-covered combination prescription on the shipped data.

Measured through the real `validate` over `DrugReferenceTestSupport.shippedEntries()`, head `d8db2a90` against this change. One `Dorzolamide / Timolol` order (codes `S01ED51`, uncovered, and `S01EC03`) asked *"Can I give her timolol and levobunolol?"* read `Levobunolol interacts with active order timolol` beside `Levobunolol is in the same ATC class (S01ED) as active order Dorzolamide (ophthalmic)` — dorzolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, not an S01ED beta blocker — where both the merge base and this change print `Dorzolamide / Timolol` in all four sentences. One `Ibuprofen / Famotidine` order (`M01AE51`, uncovered, and `A02BA03`) asked about ibuprofen, ketoprofen and suprofen named that ONE prescription **four** ways under round 6's reading — `famotidine`, `ibuprofen`, `Famotidine`, `famotidine` — two of them under an M01AE claim famotidine does not answer; this change prints `Ibuprofen / Famotidine` in all five. **So round 6 was not self-consistent either**: a rule chip steps back to the rule's TOKEN and a class-only chip to `soleSubstanceOf`'s SUBSTANCE, and those are the same string only where the token names that substance — which the ORDER rung, unlike the ENTRY rung, never proves.

Population: 396 synthetic arrangements, one per level-4 subgroup the shipped data populates with at least two substances, each a chart carrying one partly-covered combination order whose uncovered code is in that subgroup and whose covered code belongs to a substance outside it, asked about the displayed constituent and a second subgroup member. Class sentences naming a drug that does not publish the subgroup they cite: **397 at `d8db2a90`** (one arrangement raises two), **0 here**. The reviewer's independently-built sweep of the same shape read 561 of 594 and 0 at the merge base.

**And the refusal read the QUESTION, so it made a prescription's name question-dependent** — the ticket's shape (b), which this decision claims to close. `chipSubjectRows` was built from the question's own drugs, so the same Cosopt chart printed the display in both sentences for *"Can I give her levobunolol?"* and `timolol` / `Dorzolamide (ophthalmic)` once the question also named timolol. `theSamePairIsNamedTheSameWayWhicheverQuestionReachedIt` cannot see it: its arrangement raises no refusal.

**The invariant is now pinned on the TRUTH and at both surfaces, which it never was** — the reviewer's own point was that nothing in the suite could see a false class claim, and that is how rounds 5 and 6 shipped green. `PartialOrderCoveragePartnerTest.everyClassSentenceAboutAPartlyCoveredOrderNamesADrugThatPublishesTheCitedSubgroup` (class-ONLY, worded from `classPartnerName`) and `.aFoldedClassSentenceAboutAPartlyCoveredOrderNamesADrugThatPublishesTheCitedSubgroup` (FOLDED, worded from the fold's chosen name) drive the real `validate` over the shipped KB and assert of every `is in the same ATC class (X) as active order Y` sentence that some loaded entry filed under X answers to Y — resolved through the dataset rather than against a literal, so a knowledge-base refresh cannot weaken them silently. Mutated at review round 11's head, and stated as the mutations applied THERE rather than as the mechanisms rounds 5 and 6 shipped — those were gated refusals and these are the rungs themselves, which is why `theMergedPartnerIsNotNamedAfterHalfOfACombination` survived the rounds and does not survive the first of these. Electing on the ORDER rung at `classPartnerName` reddens **both** of them, while reconciling onto the rule's token at `reconciledPartnerName`'s ORDER rung reddens the **folded** one and leaves the class-only one green — that asymmetry is the discriminator worth keeping, since it says the two cases are not one guard. Neither mutation is confined to that class and no count is published for either. `theMergedPartnerIsNotNamedAfterHalfOfACombination` reddens on the first and **not** on the second, because it asserts a label and its arrangement is one where every candidate name is truthful — which is why round 7's own cases are stated over the class SENTENCE.

**What is given up is the READING round 3 objected to**, not a claim: a lead naming a prescription that contains the chip's own subject as well as its partner (`Isoniazid interacts with active order Isoniazid / Rifapentine`) looks like a drug interacting with itself. The prescription really does hold both drugs and the mechanism prose names the interacting agent, so nothing false is asserted; and it is ONE name for one prescription, invariant across the questions that reach it, which is what #339 asks for. The alternatives were weighed and are worse. Keeping the refusal and adding a "does the constituent publish the cited subgroup" conjunct is per CLASS CLAIM while the printed name must be per PRESCRIPTION-and-RESPONSE: an unfolded rule chip has no class claim to test, a folded one has its subject's, and a class-only chip a third subject's, so the conjunct answers differently for three chips about one prescription and re-creates the ticket's defect (and it cannot be lifted to the partner without knowing every subject's class relationship before any chip is worded — the second pass the ENTRY-rung residue below already names). Keeping round 3's per-chip refusal is round 4's own measured defect. Reverting only round 6 leaves a folded chip's shared name on the rule's token, which is false in the `Ibuprofen / Famotidine` arrangement above, and leaves rule and class chips disagreeing for every refused partner.

**One arrangement is worse than round 6 left it, and it is the one where no truthful single name exists.** Where the fold DECLINES because the rule's token does not name the prescription (the `naproxen`-rule-under-an-`Esomeprazole 20mg`-order shape, whose free text disagrees with its own concept's codes — #293), the rule sentence keeps the token and the class sentence takes `OrderPartner.label`, so the chip reads `Ibuprofen interacts with active order naproxen … is in the same ATC class (M01AE) as active order Esomeprazole 20mg`. Round 6 printed `naproxen` / `Naproxen` there. That is a two-name response and the class sentence names a drug the cited subgroup does not classify — but it is `nameByOrder`'s own accepted residue rather than something this decision introduces: the merge base printed exactly this (measured through the same fixture in a worktree at `abb36813`), and it is already pinned AS WRONG, on its own arrangement, by `NonCodedDrugOrderNameTest.aClassChipCanNameAnOrderAfterTextTheCitedSubgroupDoesNotClassify`. Round 6 repaired it only as a side effect of a mechanism that broke the ordinary case; closing it needs the display-versus-codes disagreement decided at the builder, which is that ticket's business and not this one's.

### Measured

Through the real `DrugSafetyValidator.validate` over the SHIPPED knowledge base (`DdiDrugReferenceSource.load()`, 2283 entries), the ticket's own question and the seven orders its seven chips name — the ticket reports eight active orders and lists seven chips; the eighth raises none against hydrocortisone — A/B against the same head with the reconciliation disabled:

| chip | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| rule arm × 3 | `active order celecoxib` / `diclofenac` / `ibuprofen` | `Celecoxib` / `Diclofenac` / `Ibuprofen` |
| class arm × 4 | `active order Dexamethasone` / `Prednisone` / `Budesonide` / `Methylprednisolone` | unchanged |

Existing-test impact, taken from the compiler rather than estimated: **1603 tests, 8 failures in 5 classes** on a prototype without the index; seven are the partner name moving and the eighth is the flatness regression the index closes. A grep for `active order <lowercase>` matches a much larger population than that, because most of its hits are javadoc, comments and chips nothing reconciles — so do not size this change from one. Apply the change and read the failures.

Screening-arm cost, counted by a `getAll()`-counting subclass. Over the pinned 16-entry excerpt with 8 active orders and the shared screening question: dataset calls attributable to the orders **8 → 17**, chips unchanged at 10. **Re-measured over the shipped KB with a 43-order chart, because the excerpt understates it by about 6×**: **53 → 105** calls, and **~+9 ms** per pass (53.6 vs 44.3 ms medians, 20 interleaved runs), of which the ladder is ~6.4 ms and the 342 reconciliations ~1.3 ms — ~4.4 µs each. A request pays that **twice**, pre-answer and post-answer, each pass building its own `CoMedications`: ~19 ms and two index builds on that chart. On a screening question `inPlay` is empty, so `addInteractionWarnings` never runs and `CoMedications.resolved()` was previously called zero times; this is one ladder resolution plus one index build per pass, constant in the number of pairs and linear in the orders.

The index is decisively worth it rather than merely affordable. Same arrangement, index against the walk it replaced, chips byte-identical in every cell: 1 drug in play 17.1 vs 24.6 ms, 2 drugs 19.4 vs 40.4, 5 drugs 23.5 vs 81.8, 10 drugs 37.3 vs 163.1, screening 56.4 vs **257.0**. One index build is ~963 µs and one old-style ask ~667 µs, so two asks pay for it and a screening pass makes 342. The drug-in-play path is a wash: cross-JVM against `09717dc7`, three sessions of 25 interleaved runs, `inPlay(1)` medians 14.8/16.2/15.9 ms at HEAD against 15.7/16.2/18.1 at base, and `inPlay(5)` 21.4/23.2/23.4 against 23.3/26.0/26.9 — HEAD first in both, so HEAD is at or below base in every session. **Rebuild the arrangement before trusting the µs figures here**: it is the 43-order chart of Decision 55 (16 orders carrying their entry's own ATC codes, 27 by name only) over the shipped KB, and the in-play drug list is the excerpt's own `IN_PLAY` order.

### Trade-offs

- **+** One response names one active order one way wherever the module can PROVE the two names denote one drug, and the same pair is named the same way whichever question reached it. Both of the ticket's measured shapes close.
- **+** **A partly-covered fixed-dose combination is named by its own display on EVERY chip of the response, and no chip states a class its named drug does not publish** (review round 7). That is a strictly stronger position than the merge base's on both counts: the base named such a prescription by the rule's token on its unfolded rule chips and by the display on its class ones, and rounds 5 and 6 of this review had it named by a constituent under a subgroup the constituent does not answer. Measured over 396 arrangements (see **What the widening cost the gate**): 397 false class sentences at `d8db2a90`, 0 here.
- **+** No new mis-attribution class exists: both movements of the gate NARROW what the widened call sites would otherwise print (see **What the widening cost the gate**). The refusal is reached down the new path and pinned there (`aRuleWhoseTokenNamesTwoSubstancesKeepsItsOwnTokenOnAnUnfoldedChipToo`).
- **+** `unambiguouslyNames` gets cheaper from the SECOND reconciliation of a pass onward: one dataset walk per pass in place of one per reconciliation, including the folded ones it already served. A pass making exactly one reconciliation pays ~963 µs for the build against ~667 µs for the ask it replaces, so that pass is ~1.4× dearer; every pass this change created makes many.
- **−** **Decision 39's name-union bound does NOT transfer, and this decision retires it for unfolded chips.** That bound rested on the folded chip's class sentence already carrying the ladder's display, so the prompt's name union shrank rather than grew. An unfolded chip has no class sentence, so for a rule-only partner the ladder name was not in the prompt at all and the rule's token can be replaced outright — Decision 39 measured 2,406 of 513,026 gate-satisfying rules whose handed-out label does not contain the token. The chip reaches the prompt verbatim through `DrugReferenceInjector.renderFinding`, so this is prompt-visible movement. What survives is the weaker half that #297 actually needs: the note's name is a word of the chip's, so the two surfaces cannot disagree.
- **−** **Decision 39's other accepted cost now reaches unfolded chips too**: the name a chip prints for an order need not be a string the CHART carries. `Aspirin 81mg` is printed `Acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin)`, which is the dataset's row rather than the prescription. That is not introduced here — the class arm already printed exactly that for exactly that order — but the ticket's own rationale for picking a convention ("it is what the clinician sees in the chart") is only satisfied on the rungs where the ladder's name IS the order's display.
- **−** **A rule whose partner `activeOrderEntryFor` cannot resolve keeps the token**, because `reconciledPartnerFor` declines on a null `SubjectRule.partner`. That is one of two lookup conditions — see the next bullet for the other, which review round 2 found and which is not narrow — and it is narrower than "the dataset covers no entry for the order": an order carrying an uncovered code is still reached through `OrderPartner.substances` and does reconcile (measured on the shipped KB — an order displayed `Aspirin 81mg` with an uncovered code prints `Aspirin 81mg`, where it printed `aspirin` before). A FOLDED chip is outside this altogether — it hands the class hit's own partner straight to `reconciledPartnerName` — which is why `ClassChipPartnerLabelTest.anOrderTheDatasetDoesNotCoverIsNamedByItsOwnDisplayName` witnesses the folded half and **not** this residue, and nothing in the suite pins the unfolded half of it. The invariant delivered is therefore "one name wherever the module can prove it", not "one name always", and the alternative is asserting an identity it cannot prove, which is the #161/#187/#194 failure.
- **−→+** **`SubjectRule.partner` and the co-medication list are two resolutions of ONE chart and they do not agree, which round 1 shipped as a silent new instance of the ticket's own defect.** `SubjectRule.partner` comes from `activeOrderEntryFor` over `findForActiveOrders` (ATC ∪ NAME, additive by design); the index it is looked up in is built from `orderPartners` (the chart's ATC-code walk, then the orders no code reached resolved by NAME). So one PRESCRIPTION can resolve to two reference substances with a partner keyed on only one of them, the lookup answers null for the second, and that chip keeps `partnerLabel` beside another chip about the same prescription that reconciled. The shipped KB files `Ketoconazole` and `Levoketoconazole` as two substances (two `drugbank_id`s) publishing one `rxnorm_name` and one identical ATC list, so a chart carrying a single mapped `Ketoconazole` order resolves both: measured through the real `validate` over `DdiDrugReferenceSource.load()`, `Abacavir interacts with active order Ketoconazole` beside `Ketoconazole interacts with active order ketoconazole` in one chip list — the ticket's own shape (a), which `DrugReferenceInjector.renderFinding` copies verbatim into the prompt as two citable `safety_finding` records naming one prescription two ways. **`CoMedications.partnerNaming` therefore has a third rung**: the co-medication this pass attributed a CHART-recorded ATC code that the entry also publishes to. That is not a claim the two are one substance — `substanceKey` exists because this KB publishes one `A02BC05` for `Omeprazole` and `Esomeprazole` alike — it is the inverse of `findByActiveOrders`' own admission predicate, and `unambiguouslyNames` still decides separately whether the name may be printed, so the rung can only turn a chip that printed the token into one the gate is asked about. Scoped to the codes the CHART records, because a partner reached by NAME carries the DATASET's codes for a whole substance; nothing in the suite pins that conjunct (measured — mutate it out and the api build stays green), and it is kept because only a charted code can have admitted anything. Where an entry publishes charted codes of two prescriptions the entry's own first such code decides, the presentation choice `orderCarrying` already makes. `OneOrderNameAcrossOneResponseTest.aPartnerEntryTheLadderKeyedNoCoMedicationOnStillNamesItsPrescriptionOnce` is the pin, over a verbatim shipped-KB slice; return the substance lookup alone and it is the one case in the api suite that reddens.

  **Measured, through the production accessors and not a re-expression of them.** `DrugReferenceService.findForActiveOrders` over a one-order chart for each of the shipped KB's **2114** substances: **84** of them resolve to more than that substance. Sweeping all 84 through the real `validate` against up to three counterpart drugs each — **216 responses**, flagging any response in which two different `active order` labels denote one prescription (a label denotes it when it repeats the order's display or when `findImpliedByDrugName` gives it a substance in common with the display's): with the rule-arm reconciliation disabled altogether **94** divergent and **7** of them differing only in CASE; at round 1's head **100** and **6**; with this rung **94** and **0**. So the rung removes every response round 1 added — the six are the `Ketoconazole` and `Dexfenfluramine` families, and the head-only set is empty against the disabled head — and closes one case-divergence the pre-#339 code had.

  **What it does NOT close is the other 94, and they are a gate refusal rather than a lookup miss.** They are the same 94 with the reconciliation disabled, so nothing here made them: they are orders whose NAME implies a second substance the chart's codes do not reach (`Mecasermin rinfabate` → `Mecasermin`, `Melphalan flufenamide` → `Melphalan`, `Asparaginase Escherichia coli` → `Asparaginase Erwinia chrysanthemi`). A fourth rung indexing each partner under every substance its order's display implies was **implemented and measured**: the sweep is byte-identical, 94 and 0, with the divergent set unchanged line for line — because `unambiguouslyNames` then refuses, the rule's token being the OTHER substance's own display name. It was reverted. Closing those means weakening the gate, which is the #161/#187/#194 mis-attribution this decision refuses to open.

- **−→+** **The widening gave one prescription two chips that say the same thing, and review round 12 found it.** A fixed-dose combination prescription is ONE order-rung co-medication — `CoMedications.partnerNaming` maps every constituent entry to it through `OrderPartner.substances` — while `bestRulePerPartner` keys a rule on the partner ENTRY, so a subject the data rules on for two constituents raises two chips. Naming both after the prescription rather than after their two rule tokens removed the only thing telling them apart wherever the knowledge base rates the two rules alike and files them under one class-level mechanism note, and the identical sentence then reached the clinician twice and the prompt twice as two numbered, citable `safety_finding` records keyed alike by `ChartSearchAiUtils.resourceKey`. Nothing threw, no chip count looked wrong and no test reddened. Measured through the real `validate` over the shipped knowledge base: one `Emtricitabine / Tenofovir disoproxil` order on `J05AR03` asked *"Can I give her bedaquiline?"* rendered `Bedaquiline interacts with active order Emtricitabine / Tenofovir disoproxil — Moderate. Coadministration of bedaquiline with other agents known to induce hepatotoxicity may potentiate the risk of liver injury.` twice, where the merge base rendered `active order tenofovir disoproxil` and `active order emtricitabine` — the ticket's own "de-duplicating by eye" cost, in mirror image.

  **Closed by `DrugSafetyValidator.StatedInteractionChips`**, a per-pass ledger of the chips this pass has already STATED, in the words it stated them in, asked at both active-order rule arms. It is deliberately not `InteractionPairs`, whose own javadoc says why a repeat must not be recognised by rendered text: that ledger answers "has a chip been raised for this PAIR" and text equality UNDER-recognises a repeat two arms word differently. This one answers the opposite question — two DIFFERENT pairs that render alike — and both run. It is not `SafetyWarning.equals` either, which deliberately does not exist so that nothing DOWNSTREAM can collapse chips this module meant to keep apart (`InteractionRouteVariantTest.eachCollapsedChipIsInjectedIntoThePromptExactlyOnce`); the decision stays in the validator, where the two arms that create the duplicate are. Three details are load-bearing. The key is every field the chip's sentence is made of — the `type`, `drug`, `detail` and `severity` it renders with, plus the two booleans `renderFinding` reads. Not every field a consumer can read: Decision 70 added a fifth wire key, `chartOrderBridges`, deliberately outside this one (Decision 64). `InteractionPairs.add` stays OUTSIDE the collapse, because the pair really was reported under the surviving chip's words and the screening arm must go on standing down from it. And in the screening arm the collapse is applied where the candidate is COLLECTED rather than after the cap, so a restatement is not counted into `PairChipExtent` as a pair found and withheld (Decision 60/#336). Since Decision 65 the drug-in-play arm's own collapse has that consequence too — what it returns for the extent is the rule chips it appended, i.e. after this ledger has dropped a restatement — and there the two coincide by construction rather than by placement, because that arm applies no cap for a collapse to fall on the wrong side of. That third one is the half with a wire consequence, and review round 13 found it asserted in three places and pinned by none: `aScreenOfACombinationPrescriptionStatesOneRelationshipOnce` now reads the extent through the same `Sink` `PairChipExtentContextTest` drives, and moving the collapse into the emission loop makes it report `found=2, reported=2` beside one chip. The second — `InteractionPairs.add` outside the collapse — is defence in depth rather than load-bearing, on that round's measurement: moving it inside is green and it could construct no arrangement where the output differs, because the ledger spans both arms and drops the re-reported chip anyway.

  **Measured over a population read out of the shipped data rather than chosen.** The ARRANGEMENTS were selected by reading the knowledge-base file directly — a script over the raw JSON, and deliberately not a re-expression of any production predicate, because nothing it decides is quoted as a property of the module: 1444 distinct CIEL cross-reference names containing ` / `, of which 846 have every ` / `-separated part equal (lower-cased) to some row's `name` or `rxnorm_name`, of which 610 have at least one third drug whose interaction rows against two of the constituents carry the same severity AND the same mechanism text. Every figure BELOW is production's, from the real `validate` and the real `injectRecords`. Driving one arrangement per product through the real `validate` over the shipped KB — the product as a single active order whose only ATC code is uncovered, asked `Can I give her <subject>?` — **440 of the 610 raise at least one chip**, and the chip totals are: merge base `e9109a58` **939 chips, 0 byte-identical duplicates**; this branch before round 12 **939 chips, 366 duplicates across 345 of the 610**; with the ledger **573 chips, 0 duplicates**. So every chip the collapse removes is a restatement and the duplication is entirely this decision's own. **The injected `drug_reference` records are untouched by it**: over the same 610 arrangements, driven through the real `injectRecords`, every rendered `drug_reference` text is byte-identical with the ledger and without it (636 records, 0 differing lines) — the collapse removes a `safety_finding` and nothing else. That was measured rather than argued, because `DrugReferenceInjector.reconciledPartnerNoteName` finds a chip by RULE IDENTITY, so a collapsed chip's rule falls back to `partnerLabel`; on the ORDER rung, which is the rung a combination prescription reaches, `reconciledPartnerName` already hands the note that same `partnerLabel`, so the fallback lands on the value it would have carried. What the sweep establishes is the OUTPUT — the records did not move on this population — and not that no other rung exists: the ENTRY rung with two rows of one substance as two partners would differ, and this population says nothing about whether it is reachable. `OneOrderNameAcrossOneResponseTest.oneCombinationPrescriptionStatesOneRelationshipOnce` and `.oneCombinationPrescriptionInjectsOneCitableFinding` pin the drug-in-play arm and its prompt, `.aScreenOfACombinationPrescriptionStatesOneRelationshipOnce` the screening arm, all three over a verbatim shipped-KB slice (`ddi-combination-two-rules-one-note.json`) so a knowledge-base refresh leaving that family alone cannot silently retire them. Removing the gate at `addInteractionWarnings`' emission reddens the first two; removing it at `addActiveOrderPairInteractions`' candidate collection reddens the third.

  **What the collapse gives up is WHICH constituent, and it gives it up on the chip alone.** The injected `drug_reference` record still lists each partner under the rule's own token, which is this decision's own prompt-level residue (the order-driven-record bullet above), so both constituents are still named to the model. What no surface states any more is that TWO rules fired. **The alternative — naming the prescription once and saying which half the rule is about — was declined**: it is new clause structure in a sentence `DrugSafetyChipLabelTest` and issue #108 constrain and that `DrugReferenceInjector.renderFinding` copies verbatim into a citable `safety_finding`; the constituent it would print is the rule's own token, which falls back to a bare ATC code (`partnerLabel`), the absence of a name that Decisions 38/39 keep out of a chip; and applying it only where a duplicate would otherwise occur makes one chip's wording depend on what OTHER chips the response holds, which is the response-level conditioning rounds 5 to 7 of this review already paid for once. The ticket's complaint is about names, not clauses.

- **−** Seven existing cases changed their expected partner name. Each keeps its strictness and its subject; `OneNameAcrossChipAndInjectedRecordTest.anUnfoldedChipsPartnerKeepsTheRulesOwnTokenInTheNote` was RENAMED, because its name stated the invariant this decision removes and a case named after the old answer would state something false while passing. It now asserts the property (chip and note name one partner one way), which is what #297 is about and is strictly stronger than the pair of literals it replaced.
- **−** The screening arm now resolves the co-medication ladder where it resolved nothing, which is new work on the pre-answer pass of exactly the question shape Decision 54's laziness was written for. One resolution per pass is the cost that decision established as acceptable; it is not one per pair.
- **−** `DrugReference.nameKeys()` is a third derived view of the alias list beside `foldedAliases`. It is derived in `setAliases`, the sole writer, so #172 does not reach it — but it is a set rather than an index-aligned list, and nothing may read a witness out of it by index. `NameIndexAgreesWithIsNamedTest` asks of whole loaded datasets that it agrees with `isNamed`, because the claimant set is what decides whether one substance's rated mechanism may be printed under another's name.
- **−** **An ORDER-DRIVEN `drug_reference` record keeps the rule's token in its interaction notes, so one prompt can still carry one prescription under two names.** Such a record has no interaction chip behind it and renders its own entry's rules, whose `Interaction` objects are not the ones any chip carries — so `DrugReferenceInjector.reconciledPartnerNoteName`'s rule-identity test never matches and every note falls back to `partnerLabel`. Harmless while an unfolded chip printed `partnerLabel` too; not harmless now. Measured through the real `injectRecords` over the pinned excerpt, a patient on Warfarin, Acetylsalicylic acid and Digoxin asked *"Can I give her ibuprofen?"*: the in-play `Ibuprofen` record lists `Warfarin` while the order-driven `Acetylsalicylic acid` record lists `warfarin`, where before this change both read `warfarin`. **This is why the ticket's invariant is claimed for the CHIP LIST it measures and not for the whole prompt.** **Its SIZE, because one example reads as a corner and it is not one** (review round 9). Over 200 synthetic arrangements — the first 200 entries of the shipped knowledge base publishing at least two interaction tokens `DrugReferenceService.lookupByToken` resolves to another substance, each charted as up to three of those partners as active orders through `DrugReferenceTestSupport.contextNaming` (so the real `withReferenceNames` runs) and asked `Can I give her <the entry's own name>?`, driven through the real `injectRecords`, with every `active order X` in a `safety_finding` and every note label in a `drug_reference` record's `Interactions:` section grouped by `DrugReference.substanceGroupKey()` — one prompt names one substance two ways in **20 of the 200** at this head against **2 of 200** at the merge base (`e9109a58`), 28 substance-level divergences against 5. **None is a false claim and none is two unrelated strings**: 15 of the 28 differ only in case (`Metoclopramide` / `metoclopramide`), 13 have one name inside the other, 0 are unrelated. **And only 16 of the 28 are this bullet's shape** — excluding the order-driven records' own notes leaves 12, of which 11 are the chip's `DrugReference.displayLabel()` against the record's own `getName()` (`Levosalbutamol (levalbuterol)` beside `Levosalbutamol`), the two-vocabularies residue Decision 51 already accepts for a folded chip and now reaching unfolded ones, and one a bare case difference (`Ketorolac` / `ketorolac`); at the merge base all 5 are this bullet's shape. Re-measure rather than carrying these figures: they are a property of the shipped dataset and of that arrangement, and the sweep was a throwaway driven from the api test tree rather than a case in the suite. Closing it means keying that lookup on the PARTNER rather than on rule identity, which needs the partner entry to travel beside the name on the `SafetyWarning` and re-opens the key-dependence question the accessor's own condition exists for (`OrderDrivenInjectionResolutionTest.oneOrderInjectsOneRecordSetWhicheverWayItResolves`) — a separate change, and one #297 already tried and abandoned in a neighbouring form.

Measured through the real `validate` over the pinned excerpt: chip `active order Warfarin`, note `warfarin`, where before #339 both read `warfarin`. Decision 51 already accepted exactly this for a FOLDED chip on that shape; this widens the reach and not the kind, and `OneOrderNameAcrossOneResponseTest.onAFlattenedChartTheChipIsReconciledAndTheNoteIsNot` pins it as current behaviour. A real patient gets the other branch — `PatientClinicalContextBuilder` attaches per-order structure for every chart it can read.

What round 3 recorded as this bullet's own residue — the prescription named by the token on one chip and by its display on another — does NOT come back with it, because nothing refuses the display any more: one prescription, one name, for every chip of the response.

## Appendix A: Measurements whose only home was `CLAUDE.md`

`CLAUDE.md` was trimmed to directives and pointers (2026-08-31); it had grown from 5 KB to 159
KB in twenty-six days, 94% of it drug-safety narrative, with one bullet at 39,603 characters
whose bulk was the review rounds of #339. The reasoning it carried is in the decisions above and
in the javadoc — `DrugSafetyValidator` is 74% comment lines, `DrugReference` 69%. These figures
were the exception. Every `N of M` / `N → M` ratio in that file was extracted and checked
against `api/src`, `omod/src`, `eval/` and this document; the six below had no other home, and
the seventh — the #339 sweep — is recorded only for the two figures Decision 63 does not carry.
Each sits under the rule it was measured for. The check was pattern-based, so a measurement
phrased outside those two shapes could have been missed.

**The ATC dictionary is sparse and the reference data is not** (#151, #228; Decisions 54, 58).
Measured 2026-08-13 by the predicate `PatientClinicalContextBuilder.addAtcCodes` applies (a
concept-reference-source name containing `ATC`): **27 of the 43** active drug orders on the
3.7.1 demo instance carry no ATC code at all, while `DrugReference.normalizedAtcCodes()` over
the real `DdiDrugReferenceSource.parse` of the 19 MB knowledge base publishes codes for 1839
of its 2283 entries. The sparsity is the dictionary's, never the reference data's — which is
why `findByActiveOrders` is package-private and `findForActiveOrders` (ATC ∪ name, and ∪ bridged concept since Decision 68) is the list
every consumer takes.

**What the name leg of `addPartnersForUnmappedOrders` bought** (#228; Decision 54). Through the
real `validate` over that knowledge base and the standalone's own order sets: 14 partners → 42,
and patients with at least one partner **12 of 24 → 24 of 24**.

**Resolving a partner across the whole dataset instead of against the patient's own orders**
(#188). It merges genuinely distinct partners on **397 of the 2283** entries (`trastuzumab`
with `trastuzumab deruxtecan`), which in a record costs a partner its name. The bound is what
makes `activeOrderEntryFor` safe: resolution is against the patient's own orders, so wherever
it merges two labels the chip merged them first.

**Why `nameMatchStrength` is not re-ranked by alias length** (#192). Longest-alias repairs
**43 of 54** mis-resolutions and breaks 34 that earliest-match gets right. Preferring
`canonicalRow` instead renames a charted `Ketorolac (ophthalmic)` allergy and regresses #187.

**How incomplete #161's hand-picked `UNCLASSIFYING_ATC_GROUPS` was** (#263; Decision 34). Its
hardening reproduced the defect it was fixing: **46 of 1090** ROW pairs named a missing group,
21 of them moved there by the fix; over SUBSTANCE pairs — the other base `sharedClass` defines
— that is **19 of 319**, with 2 of those moved there by the fix.

**What Decision 55 measured and declined.** `normalizeName`'s own re-derivation runs 2,141 to
143,533 calls against 1.42M–1.93M folds, so it was not worth hoisting beside the operand folds.

**The #339 order-rung sweep — the control arm only.** Decision 63 carries this sweep and a
larger one; what it does not state is the arrangement's base and its disabled-head control, so
only those are recorded here. Measured through `findForActiveOrders`, **84 of the shipped KB's
2114 substances** resolve to more than themselves on a one-order chart, and that set of 84 is
what the sweep's 216 responses were generated from. Against the reconciliation DISABLED the same
sweep reads **94 divergent responses and 7 case-only divergences** — so the rung removes every
response the widening added and adds none. See Decision 63 for the head-to-head figures and the
reproduction method.

**A note on suite-size denominators.** The trimmed file drops the quoted totals (1058, 1171,
1173, 1192, 1347/1350, 1585) because every one had gone stale against a suite that held about 1596 `@Test` methods when this was written (2026-08-31). Where a measurement's force depends on a denominator, state the
denominator *and* the date, here rather than in `CLAUDE.md`.

## Decision 64: A finding states which of this patient's own orders each substance it names was resolved from

**Status: Accepted** (September 2026) — implemented, issue [#349](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-module-chartsearchai/issues/349).

### Context

#349 reports a `/search` response whose answer DENIES what its own chip asserts. Measured on the 3.7.1 standalone at `main` @ `77c0f9a2` over the bundled DDInter knowledge base, three runs identical: a patient with two active orders whose only chart names are the local brands `Zolvimix` (mapped `C10AA01` + `J01FA09`) and `Klarizom` (mapped `J01FA09`), asked *"Are any of his current medications interacting with each other?"*, returned `pairs: {"found": 1, "reported": 1}` and one Major chip reading `Simvastatin interacts with active order Clarithromycin — Major. Coadministration with potent inhibitors of CYP450 3A4 …` beside the answer *"The records do not address interactions between the patient's current medications."*

**It is not a missing injection**, and the ticket rules that out with the module's own DEBUG line: `Injected 0 active-order, 0 drug-reference (0 chars) and 1 safety-finding record(s) — reference slice 1 record(s), 363 chars`. The finding reached the prompt. `references: []` says the answer cited nothing.

The cause is that the finding names two substances the chart spells nowhere. The module reached both through their WHO ATC maps — `withReferenceNames` fills `getActiveDrugReferenceNames()` from `findForActiveOrders`, which is what lets `hasActiveDrug` join a rule token to a brand-named order at all (#136) — and that mapping appears nowhere in the prompt. So the record asserts a relationship between two substances while stating nothing about what in this chart it is a relationship about, and the model resolves that by disclaiming. Nothing else in that prompt could have supplied the connection: a screening question names no drug, so `DrugReferenceInjector.matchingEntries` scopes in no `drug_reference` record, and the chart already substantiated both orders by uuid, so `unrepresentedActiveOrders` injected none either — which is exactly what the two zeroes in the DEBUG line say.

**The ticket's own account of the naming path is wrong, and the correction matters for the next reader.** It says #339's `namesNamingOrder` gate declined. It cannot have: `J01FA09` IS a code the loaded KB names, so `orderPartners`' walk takes the ENTRY rung (`entry != null` → `new OrderPartner(entry)`), `unnameableCode` is false, `nameByOrder` is never called and `OrderPartner.namingOrder` stays null — so `reconciledPartnerName` returns at its ENTRY rung and prints the dataset's own name. The conclusion the ticket draws is unaffected: the printed name is the knowledge base's, it is correct, and Decision 63's review rounds 5–7 are canonical for why it must not be re-decided.

### Decision

The injected `safety_finding` states the bridge the module already established, as one additional sentence between the detail and the strength clause: `DrugReferenceInjector.FINDING_CHART_ORDER_LEAD` followed by `"; "`-joined `"<Substance> from <order display>"` items. On the ticket's own chart the record becomes `… metabolized by the isoenzyme. This module resolved the substances named here from this patient's own active orders. Simvastatin from Zolvimix; Clarithromycin from Klarizom. This finding is a reason to withhold it.` — the lead ENDS a sentence, which is a fidelity decision and not a style one; see the residue below.

Additive, prompt-facing only, and monotone: it adds words and moves no call. (Decision 70 later publishes the same attributions as each chip's `chartOrderBridges` key, so "prompt-facing only" is this decision's scope and not a standing property; the chip's own `detail` is still untouched.) The chip's detail, its rank, `getSeverity()`, `licensesWithholding` and the `safetyWarnings` wire shape are untouched — #283's own scoping, and `InteractionFindingChartOrderBridgeTest.theChipDetailIsTheWordsItAlwaysWas` is that invariant.

**Why the wording is a RESOLUTION and not an identity.** "Clarithromycin from Zolvimix" says this module read that substance off that order. It is true of a combination brand carrying several substances' codes, and it deliberately does not say the prescription IS the substance nor that the substance's class classifies the prescription — the false claim Decision 63's reverted rounds 5–6 made by naming a constituent, in this very text, which `renderFinding` copies verbatim into a citable record carrying `STRENGTH_WITHHOLD`. So the clause sits beside the printed name rather than replacing it, and nothing in the naming ladder is consulted.

**The lead ENDS a sentence and the items are their own, which is a fidelity decision.** `ReferenceProseFidelityCheck` treats a record sentence reproduced WHOLE as faithful however the answer goes on, and covers the seam and not a clause's interior. The lead clears that check's `MIN_REPRODUCED_WORDS` of 12 on its own — 14 words by the check's OWN tokenizer, which splits `patient's`, and 13 by whitespace; the threshold is in the tokenizer's units — so introducing the items with a COLON would put invariant boilerplate inside a sentence whose interior carries order displays the live model is on record paraphrasing and misspelling. Ending it restores the exit for the half that never varies; the items' interior is still uncovered, which is inherent to carrying variable content. An earlier draft of this decision used the colon form in the example above.

**The SUBJECT is attributed against every order; the PARTNER only against the orders its own arm let witness it, and the CALLER supplies that set.** `activeOrdersOtherThan` drops the subject's own orders before the partner is witnessed, precisely so one prescription cannot report the two halves of one tablet as an interacting pair — its javadoc records the measured case, one `Aspirin and omeprazole` order reporting `Acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) interacts with active order esomeprazole — Minor`. So `addActiveOrderPairInteractions` hands `ordersOtherThan`, which is that reduction under its own predicate (`resolvesFromAny`); naming an order it refused would put the suppressed witness back into citable text. On the ticket's own chart, where the combination brand carries BOTH codes, that is the difference between the two items above and a third reading `Clarithromycin from Zolvimix`. The plan proposed the unscoped form and its refutation gate refused it on exactly that ground; `.eachSubstanceIsAttributedOnlyToTheOrderThePassResolvedItFrom` is the pin.

**And the reduction belongs to the ARM that performed it, which the first implementation got wrong.** `addInteractionWarnings` applies no `activeOrdersOtherThan` reduction — its own comment says it runs "ungated, uncapped, and without that arm's `activeOrdersOtherThan` reduction" — so `chartOrderBridges` performing the reduction itself, for both arms, suppressed a witness that arm had not suppressed. Measured through the real `injectRecords` over the verbatim DDInter slice `ddi-alias-drug-names.json`: ONE prescription carrying both `C10AA01` and `J01FA09`, asked *"Can I give him clarithromycin?"*, produced `Clarithromycin interacts with active order Simvastatin — Major. … This module resolved the substances named here from this patient's own active orders. Clarithromycin from Zolvimix. This finding is a reason to withhold it.` — Simvastatin unbridged, i.e. this issue's own unciteable finding surviving inside the clause added to close it, now beside a sentence asserting the module HAS stated its resolutions. Found by a clean-context review agent, not by the plan or either gate pass. `.aCombinationOrderCarryingBOTHSubstancesBridgesBothSides` reproduces it verbatim when the call site is mutated back. The general lesson: a shared helper that performs a caller's reduction is asserting something about a caller it cannot see.

**The silence test is the order's RECORDED NAMES against the substance, never the string the chip prints.** (Superseded by Decision 70, which narrows it to the one name a chart record DISPLAYS — the paragraph below is why it is not the PRINTED name, which that decision keeps.) The plan's first form asked `!DrugReference.matchesOrderName(order.getDisplay(), printedName)`, and that is measurably the wrong operand: `matchesOrderName` is `containsBoundedToken`, so it can only answer true where the display carries the WHOLE printed string, and a printed name is a `displayLabel()` — multi-word, parenthesized or synonym-suffixed for a large minority of this knowledge base (`Acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin)`, `Hydrocortisone (ophthalmic)`, `Emtricitabine / Tenofovir disoproxil`). Under it an order plainly named `Aspirin 81mg` would have been bridged as if the chart named nothing. `recordsANameOf` asks instead whether any name the ORDER records reaches the substance, through `matchesDrugNameAny` — the same `matchesDrugName` primitive `resolvesFrom`'s own name leg uses. So the condition is exactly "`resolvesFrom` is true and its NAME leg is not what made it true", i.e. the ATC leg alone, which is what makes the scope claim below true of the code rather than merely asserted. `.anOrderNamingTheSubstanceOnlyByAnAliasIsNotBridged` is the case that reddens if this weakens back to a printed-name test.

**Scoped to the ATC leg, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** *(Superseded by [Decision 70](#decision-70-one-prescription-is-named-one-way-across-the-answer-the-chips-and-the-wire), which is this paragraph's own subject: the premise below — that a NAME-leg resolution means the chart's own words carry the connection — is the one that decision refutes by measurement, since the recorded set carries the ordered CONCEPT's name and no `drug_order` record renders it. The silence test is now the order's DISPLAY, so the clause is no longer scoped to the ATC leg and an over-wide NAME match can print. What survives unchanged is the residue named at the end of this paragraph.)* Where the NAME leg resolved a substance, the order's own recorded names already reach it, so the chart's own words carry the connection and the model needs no help. The ATC leg is different in kind: the mapping is in no record. The residue is #136's alias-spelling shape — an order named `Acetylsalicylic acid 81mg` beside a chip printing the token `aspirin` — which is pre-existing, is Decision 63's business, and is not what this ticket reproduces.

**An order the module could read no name for contributes nothing.** `[ATC …]` is the absence of a name (#290), so handing it over would put a bare code where the record had a substance name. Asked THROUGH `displayNamesADrug`, the one place those two conditions are written (#292). `CLAUDE.md`'s "never before merely labelling" exemption does not reach this caller: nothing here is being labelled, and the refusal is the point. An earlier draft of this decision said the opposite and wrote the pair inline — the third copy that method exists to prevent — while the code called the method, so the ADR and the code disagreed about which question was asked.

**The bridge travels on the `SafetyWarning`, resolved by one shared method at each arm's chip-wording site.** The injector holds neither the arms' resolution nor which side came from which order; deriving it there would be a second walk over the same orders reaching the same answer, which is the two-resolutions-that-agree shape #151 forbids and whose failure mode is silent and one-directional. Both active-order arms get it, so it is not per-arm scoped — the mistake #283 measured for its own clause and Decision 63 measured for the reconciliation.

**It is NOT "decided once at `interactionWarning`", and three places said so before review.** That method takes the list as a parameter, so nothing structural stops an ARM resolving wrongly or not at all. The claim mattered because it implied the arms could not answer differently; the structural proof that they can is that either arm can be neutered to an empty list on its own — the drug-in-play arm reddens `.aFoldedChipsPartnerIsBridgedToo`, `.theDrugInPlayArmsPartnerIsBridgedToo` and `.aCombinationOrderCarryingBOTHSubstancesBridgesBothSides` together, the screening arm several more. **No count of the call sites is published, and an earlier draft of this paragraph published one that a later fix in this same change falsified** by merging the drug-in-play arm's folded and unfolded branches onto one resolution — the sites move with the arms, which is the whole reason not to count them.

**It does NOT join `StatedInteractionChips`' collapse key, and it was added there and reverted.** The argument for adding it was that the key should cover every field a consumer reads, the prompt being a consumer. The argument against is decisive and came from review: that key decides which chips are EMITTED, so it reaches `PairChipExtent`'s `found`/`reported` counts (the screening arm collapses where the candidate is collected, before the cap) and, through `ChartSearchAiUtils.resourceKey(type, drug)`, whether two injected findings share one resource uuid — the property `OneOrderNameAcrossOneResponseTest.oneCombinationPrescriptionInjectsOneCitableFinding` exists to hold. Keying on it would therefore make this clause decide which chips are EMITTED. (The reason as first written was "while every claim about it says it is prompt-facing only", which Decision 70 falsified by publishing the attributions; the emission argument is the one that survives it.) A collapsed chip carries the survivor's bridge, which is the same residue Decision 63 already accepts for that collapse ("what it gives up is WHICH constituent"). Reaching a divergence needs two rows of DIFFERENT substances printing one `displayLabel()`, plus rule tokens that differ and a reconciliation that succeeds. A review pass CONSTRUCTED it in a hand-authored fixture and confirmed the loser's bridge is lost without the key term — so the shape is not hypothetical, it is unreachable on shipped data: driving the real `DrugReference.displayLabel()` over all 2283 shipped rows, 0 labels occur on more than one row (measured 2026-09-01 through the production accessor, not a reimplementation of it).

### Alternatives

**Inject the `active_drug_order` record for the orders the validator resolved** — the ticket's own second suggestion. Refuted by the ticket's own evidence before any code was written: `unrepresentedActiveOrders` injects only orders the chart carries NO record for, so the DEBUG line's `0 active-order` means the chart already substantiated both. The orders are in the prompt; only the resolution is missing. And `renderActiveOrder` prints `"Active drug order: <display>."` — no substance name and no code — so even if it fired it would carry no bridge. A second record for an order already in the chart also duplicates chart evidence a medication count reads.

**Widen `LlmProvider.DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT`'s #112 clause**, whose antecedent is "a safety finding naming the drug asked about" and therefore has no anchor on a screening question. Declined on the measurement recorded beside it: added instructions in that area regress, and all three candidate arms in `eval/drift-metric/README.md` did and were reverted. Widening the RECORD adds evidence rather than an instruction, which is the mechanism #110 established.

**A per-substance clause naming every carrier of the code** — see the scoping paragraph above; refused by the refutation gate.

### Residue

- The order-driven CONTRAINDICATION arm can reach the same unciteable shape. The rendering side is type-agnostic — `renderFinding` prints whatever bridges the warning carries — but only the two active-order interaction arms populate them here.
- So can a CLASS-ONLY chip (`addInteractionWarnings`' `classOnly` list), which is built from a public `SafetyWarning` constructor and so answers an empty list by construction. Its sentence names its partner through `classPartnerName`, which on the ENTRY rung prints the dataset's own name for a brand-mapped order, so its lead is unciteable for the same reason. Not widened here: its partner is an `OrderPartner` rather than a resolved row, so the attribution needs different plumbing, and its sentence is a class claim rather than a pairwise relationship.
- `addQuestionPairInteractions` is **not** a residue of that kind, and an earlier draft of this list said it was. Its detail ends `", also named in the question"`, so both sides are spelled in the prompt by the question itself and an empty bridge is the correct answer.
- The injected `drug_reference` record's own interaction-note list (`DrugReferenceInjector.orderedInteractionNotes`) has this issue's shape and is not addressed: for a drug-NAMED question it renders `Interactions: Simvastatin (Major. …)` unbridged, in the same prompt as the bridged finding. That list is the knowledge base's own partners under the knowledge base's own names, and putting a chart order's display into it is what Decision 51 refused for the note's name; whether it should carry a bridge is a question of its own.
- On a combination brand the flat clause can name one prescription in two items (`Simvastatin from Zolvimix; Clarithromycin from Zolvimix` where the pass does not reduce it). A READING rather than a false claim, and the same trade Decision 63 settled for the lead itself.
- `ReferenceProseFidelityCheck` (#337) compares an answer against every cited reference-group record, and a `safety_finding` is in that group. **The lead's sentence-terminating form was RUN rather than argued**, through the real `LlmInferenceService.search` over the real bridged finding for the ticket's own chart: an answer reproducing the detail and the lead and then diverging logs *"found no divergence … faithful"* on the shipped form and WARNs *"reproduces 55 words … states different words inside the sentence it was copying"* on the colon form; lead-only reproductions behave the same way, WARNing at 14 words on the colon form alone. That check's own committed fixtures cannot see any of this — their charts carry no orders, so no bridge. What is still a residue to watch on a live run is the ITEMS' interior, which no wording covers.
- **What it costs in prompt characters**, which is the cost `ChartSearchAiUtils.referenceSlice` and #163/#229 track and the one an operator reads off the DEBUG line this ticket quotes: the lead is 87 characters, and on the ticket's own chart the two-item clause is 143 on a finding record that was 363, a one-item clause 116. No per-item formula is given — an earlier draft's was off by one, and the items' own length is the substance name and the order display, which the arrangement decides. (The 116 is the `Clarithromycin from Klarizom` item; the `Simvastatin from Zolvimix` one gives 113. Both are one-item clauses on this chart, so read that figure as an example rather than as the one-item cost.) There is no cap on a `safety_finding` and the item count is bounded by the patient's active orders, so a polypharmacy chart pays more — unbounded in the same dimension `MAX_INTERACTION_RENDER_CHARS` bounds for the `drug_reference` record, and not bounded here.
- **The per-subject hoist was implemented, measured and declined**, recorded so the next reader does not re-derive it. The subject-side gate answer is invariant across every chip of one subject and is already computed once per subject inside `activeOrdersOtherThan`; at the busiest 40-order arrangement `resolvesFromAny` runs 24,560 times for it and returns true 614. An order-preserving hoist (a per-call `boolean[]` plus a `ChartOrderBridge[]` indexed by order, with `rowsOfSubstance` made lazy — a local, so #172 is met by shape) was proven output-identical across ten arrangements and the whole suite, and buys 12→12 ms at 10 orders, 23→22 at 20, 81→79 at 40 and 342→315 at 80. Declined: 2 ms on a 40-order chart for a struct threaded through two arms. The remaining two-thirds of the cost is the partner side, which is genuinely per-chip.
- **Half the second payment is dead work.** (Superseded by Decision 70. What is stale is the whole ARGUMENT — the conclusion "dead work" and both premises under it, "only production reader is `chartOrderClause`" and "the wire serializer does not write it": since #347 `ChartSearchAiRestController.serializeSafetyWarnings` publishes exactly the post-answer pass's bridges, so both payments have a reader. What STANDS is the ~13 ms figure and the arrangement behind it, and this is still their only home.) `SafetyWarning.chartOrderBridges()`'s only production reader is `DrugReferenceInjector.chartOrderClause`, reached only from `preAnswerFindings`; the wire serializer does not write it and the collapse key deliberately does not read it. So the post-answer `validate` resolves every bridge and discards it — ~13 ms of the ~26. Not gated: the discriminator would have to be threaded through `validate` and that trade is unmeasured. Recorded because it is the honest denominator for both that figure and the declined hoist.
- **The cost's real denominator is the request, not the pass**, and the first version of this measurement argued from the pass's own spread. A request pays the pass twice — `LlmInferenceService` calls `injectRecords`/`preAnswerFindings` before the answer and `validate` after it — so the maximising arrangement is ~+26 ms per request, and 80 busiest orders ~+166 ms, against a request whose latency is an LLM call (this module's own record has production TTFT in minutes). Neither figure includes the knowledge-base parse, which is outside the timed region in both arms, so neither says anything about a cold first request.

## Decision 65: The interaction check that runs on the prescribing question states its extent too

**Status: Accepted** (September 2026) — implemented, issue [#356](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-module-chartsearchai/issues/356). Amends Decision 60; amended in turn by Decisions 69 and 71, which are what decide when a pairwise arm has "spoken" and what happens where the arm this fallback sits behind is the one that ceded.

### Context

Decision 60 gave the two PAIRWISE interaction arms a `PairChipExtent` and put it on the wire as `interactionPairs`, so that a truncated screen could say it was truncated and a complete one could say it was complete. Between them those two gates exclude the question a clinician actually asks before prescribing. `addQuestionPairInteractions` needs the question to resolve two or more reference drugs; `addActiveOrderPairInteractions` needs it to resolve none *and* to ask to be screened. *"Can I give this patient Lisinopril?"* resolves exactly one, so neither ran, and the arm that did the work — `addInteractionWarnings`, which screens a drug in play against the patient's own medications — stated nothing at all. What "one drug" means here is what the DATASET resolved and not what the clinician typed: a name filed under several rows (`Dexamethasone` beside `Dexamethasone (ophthalmic)`) opens the question-pair arm, which then owns the field — see the trade-off below.

#356 reproduced it live on the 3.7.1 standalone at `main` @ `9aca5790`, twice with identical results, against a patient on Lamivudine, Nevirapine and Stavudine. *"Can I give this patient Lisinopril?"* returned `{"answer": "The records do not address the suitability of Lisinopril.", "safetyWarnings": [], "interactionPairs": null}`. **The screen had run**: the Lisinopril entry resolved and was injected (`referenceSliceRecords: 1`, `referenceSliceChars: 1088`), and the identical question shape returns a Moderate chip against Nevirapine when the drug is Amlodipine. So the arm enumerated Lisinopril against all three orders, related none of them above the floor, and said so nowhere — and `null` is the value Decision 60 defines as *the producer stated no measurement*. The clinician got an abstention indistinguishable from one where nobody looked. The tell in that run's own table: of five probe cells, the only one that stated an extent was the one whose question named TWO drugs.

### Decision

**The drug-in-play arm states the extent where neither pairwise arm did** — and, since Decision 71, only where the QUESTION also resolved a drug this arm could screen. Behind a screening arm that states nothing, nothing else states the field: this fallback is gated on `questionDrugScreened`, which that arm's own `questionDrugs.isEmpty()` gate makes false. Do not read this bullet as licensing a widening to cover it; Decision 71 refuses that by name.

- **`addInteractionWarnings` returns how many pairs it related** — the rule chips it appended, after `StatedInteractionChips` has dropped any that restate one this pass already made. `validate` accumulates that and states `PairChipExtent.of(n, n)` from a fallback beside the two pairwise blocks, published through the one `recordPairExtent` call Decision 60 already established.
- **`found == reported`, because this arm applies no cap.** `maxPairChips` bounds the two quadratic arms and has never bounded this one, which raises one chip per partner it relates. It reports everything it finds, and says so.
- **Only where no pairwise arm spoke — never a sum.** A pairwise statement is about a BOUNDED list, where the two numbers may differ and the difference is the whole of what a client renders; this one cannot be bounded. Adding the two populations into two integers is the ratio-of-two-populations claim `PairChipExtent` exists to stop, published by the producer this time instead of by the client. Where a pairwise arm stated anything, its statement stands exactly as it did before.
- **The QUESTION's substances decide it, never the answer's.** `inPlay` is the question's drugs UNION the ones the answer names (echo-scoped), and the sink exists only on the post-answer pass, so a count over `inPlay` would publish the model's prose as the clinician's question — and would state an extent for a question that resolved no drug at all, whose ANSWER happened to name one. That is *"could not resolve the drug"* published as *"screened and related nothing"*, which the ticket names as the row that must not be got wrong: it would re-create #336's defect in the opposite direction. This is the property the screening arm's own gate already has, for the reason its comment gives — the pre-answer findings pass and the post-answer chips pass must not be able to disagree.
- **Unrated class relationships are chips and are not pairs.** A shared ATC subgroup or a curated cross-reactivity group raises a chip from this arm and is counted in neither number, because neither pairwise arm has a class leg at all. One wire key must not mean above-floor rule pairs on two question shapes and rule-pairs-plus-class-joins on the third. Note what "above-floor" includes: `clearsSeverityFloor` exempts an unrated RULE rather than demoting it, so a hand-authored curated rule counts here exactly as it counts on the two pairwise arms. The exclusion is of the CLASS leg, not of the unrated.
- **A chart recording no active medication states nothing.** `hasActiveMedicationRecords`, read off the context that supplies both legs their partners rather than re-derived from a partner list.

### Rejected alternatives

- **A wire key of its own.** The client contract `interactionPairs` supports — how bounded the list is, and that zero is a measurement — is the same for all three arms, and Decision 60's own settlement is that one field speaks for arms screening different populations. A second key would make every client ask which one to read.
- **Summing the arms.** Above; it is the defect this type exists to prevent.
- **Counting every interaction chip the arm raised.** It was the first draft, and refuted at plan time: it would have made `reported` a chip count on one question shape and a pair count on the other two, with nothing on the wire to tell them apart.
- **Accumulating over `inPlay` rather than the question's substances.** Also refuted at plan time, and it is the alternative that breaks the ticket's own acceptance row rather than merely blurring a number.

### Trade-offs

- **+** The commonest drug-safety question can now say its screen was complete. Before this, completeness was inferable on that shape only from the absence of a signal, which is the fail-open reading `getReferenceSlice()`'s "null is not zero" rule already refuses.
- **−** **The two arms disagree about a patient taking nothing.** `addActiveOrderPairInteractions` on a chart with no active orders returns `PairChipExtent.of(0, 0)`; the drug-in-play arm on the same chart states nothing.
